fixes.explanation: “And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man…” (Genesis 39:2). Joseph is far from home and serving in a stranger's house, but the text says the LORD is with him. Hold on to that line, friend, because it keeps showing up in this chapter. This is the heart of the whole story.
Reuben is one of Joseph's brothers (Genesis 37:21), but this verse doesn't mention him at all. Genesis 39:2 names who is with Joseph: the LORD. That's the company that matters in this verse, friend.

Potiphar is captain of the guard, so army feels like a natural guess. But verse 4 says he put Joseph in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned. Household is the word the text gives, friend. Army isn't in that verse.

“…the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s household on account of him.” (Genesis 39:5). Blessing is the word the text uses. And it didn't stop at the front door, because “The LORD’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in his house and in his field.” All of that on account of Joseph.

Warns is a natural thought, friend, but there's no warning in verse 5. It says, “…the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s household on account of him.” And the blessing reached far: “The LORD’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in his house and in his field.” Joseph's being there brought good to a house that wasn't even his.

Verse 6 says Potiphar “…did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate.” Joseph ran the whole operation, and Potiphar kept the one job of eating. Honestly, friend, if my only job were eating cookies, I'd need a bigger apron. Joseph had everything else in his care.

That's right. Joseph tells her, “No one in this house is greater than I am.” (Genesis 39:9). He's pointing out how much Potiphar has trusted him with. Then he says what Potiphar held back: “…except you, because you are his wife.”

Joseph asks, “So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9). Notice he names God in his answer. He calls it a great evil, and he calls it a sin against God. It's a clear no.

Verse 10 goes further than that. It says he “…refused to go to bed with her or even be near her.” So the refusal covered more than the act itself. And it wasn't a single no, because she spoke to him day after day.

“But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside.” (Genesis 39:12). He didn't stop to grab it. He got out of that house. I've left things behind in a hurry, friend, but never anything that mattered this much.

Verse 11 says not a single household servant was inside, so the house was empty of servants at that moment. Genesis 39:12 says he left his cloak in her hand, escaped and ran outside. Calling the servants isn't what the text says he did. The servants show up later, when she is the one who calls them (Genesis 39:14).

Shame isn't the word the text gives, friend. Genesis 39:19 says Potiphar “…burned with anger.” That comes right after he hears his wife say, “This is what your slave did to me,” so the anger lands in that moment. The text names the feeling and doesn't tell us more than that.

Genesis 39:22 says the warden put all the prisoners under Joseph's care, so Joseph is still in the prison. The verse gives him responsibility for what is done inside. Verse 23 says the warden didn't concern himself with anything under Joseph's care, because the LORD was with Joseph.
